[SECTION 1]
Distributed computing did not begin with a single invention or a single laboratory. Its roots lie in the postwar desire to make expensive computers serve many users at once and to connect machines so that they could share work, data, and storage. In the 1950s and 1960s, batch processing gave way to time-sharing systems such as MIT’s CTSS and Project MAC, which demonstrated that a central machine could support many simultaneous users. Visionaries like J.C.R. Licklider described an “Intergalactic Computer Network,” while John McCarthy imagined computing as a utility. These ideas framed computation as a resource to be accessed remotely, not merely a local appliance. The earliest distributed systems were therefore less about independent computers cooperating as equals and more about terminals, schedulers, and shared mainframes, but they established the essential premise: computation could be spread across space and coordinated through communication.

[SECTION 2]
The networking revolution of the 1960s and 1970s turned that premise into infrastructure. Paul Baran, Donald Davies, and Leonard Kleinrock developed packet switching, which broke messages into small pieces that could be routed independently and reassembled at the destination. ARPANET, launched in 1969, connected research computers and became a proving ground for remote login, file transfer, and electronic mail.
